spots: The two blue lines separate the middle area from the end zones.
Use them to describe where the play is. Rules using these lines depend on the game format.
The red line crosses the middle of the rink.
It helps you locate centre ice and describe either half of the rink.
A red line crosses the rink at each net.
Find the net opening on this line and the playable space behind it.
This spot is in the centre circle.
It is a place where the puck can be dropped to start or restart play.
Each end has two large faceoff circles with spots.
They are useful landmarks for positioning and faceoffs.
Four faceoff spots sit in the neutral zone, outside the end-zone blue lines.
Not every faceoff spot has a large circle around it.
There is a net at each end.
Know which net your team protects and which net your team attacks.
The crease is the marked area directly in front of the net.
It helps you identify the goalie’s immediate working area. Crease rules depend on the rule set.
Boards surround the ice; glass rises above them.
Use the boundary as a landmark while staying aware of nearby players.
This is the end zone containing the net your team is protecting.
Both forwards and defenders help here. Zone names change when teams switch ends.
This is the middle zone between the blue lines.
Teams move through it to connect defence and attack.
This is the end zone containing the opponent’s net.
Players can create scoring chances and support the puck here.
The central area in front of the net, between the faceoff circles.
A useful place to discuss scoring threats and protecting the middle. It is not a painted box.
The central space farther out from the net, above the lower slot.
A potential support or shooting area; the useful spot changes with pressure.
Areas just inside the attacking blue line, commonly toward either side.
Players can support an attack from here while watching for a change of possession.
Side-board areas in the end zone, between the corner and the blue-line area.
A landmark for puck support, board play and passing options.
The curved areas where the side boards meet the end boards.
Players may retrieve pucks and look for support here.
Playable ice between the net and the end boards.
The puck can move around the net; players need to track it and communicate.
The space just outside the crease in front of the net.
A place to discuss rebounds, screens and defending nearby threats.
Short marks at the sides of end-zone faceoff circles.
They help organize faceoff positioning. Exact setup follows the applicable rules.
Players enter and leave the ice through bench doors.
Changing players need clear communication and awareness. Bench locations vary.
The officials’ area and penalty benches sit along a side of the rink.
These are rink landmarks, not ordinary player support positions. Locations vary.

C.name: Centre
C.summary: Connect the play through the middle and help teammates at both ends.
C.attack: Offer a useful passing option and look for scoring space with the other forwards.
C.defend: Help protect central threats and support teammates near the puck, following your team’s coverage.
C.win: Make yourself available through the middle or another open lane as your team gains control.
C.lose: Recover toward useful defensive space and identify the most urgent threat.

LW.name: Left wing
LW.summary: A forward starting on the left side when facing the opponent’s net.
LW.attack: Create width, support the puck and move into useful scoring space. You can cross lanes when the play calls for it.
LW.defend: Help with the threats and passing lanes your team assigns. Be available when your team wins the puck.
LW.win: Offer an outlet or move into open ice with support for the new puck carrier.
LW.lose: Recover, track nearby threats and help your team protect the middle.

RW.name: Right wing
RW.summary: A forward starting on the right side when facing the opponent’s net.
RW.attack: Create width, support the puck and move into useful scoring space. You can cross lanes when the play calls for it.
RW.defend: Help with the threats and passing lanes your team assigns. Be available when your team wins the puck.
RW.win: Offer an outlet or move into open ice with support for the new puck carrier.
RW.lose: Recover, track nearby threats and help your team protect the middle.

LD.name: Left defence
LD.summary: A defender starting to the left of the partner, viewed toward the opponent’s net.
LD.attack: Support from behind the forwards and choose when joining the attack is safe.
LD.defend: Protect the net and dangerous space, manage pressure and work with your partner.
LD.win: Look for a controlled first pass or safe carry, with support available.
LD.lose: Recover your defensive shape and communicate about who pressures and who supports.

RD.name: Right defence
RD.summary: A defender starting to the right of the partner, viewed toward the opponent’s net.
RD.attack: Support from behind the forwards and choose when joining the attack is safe.
RD.defend: Protect the net and dangerous space, manage pressure and work with your partner.
RD.win: Look for a controlled first pass or safe carry, with support available.
RD.lose: Recover your defensive shape and communicate about who pressures and who supports.

G.name: Goalie
G.summary: Protect the net by tracking the puck and moving into a ready position.
G.attack: Stay engaged as your team attacks; track the play and be ready if possession changes.
G.defend: Track the puck, adjust position and prepare for a save. Communicate with teammates.
G.win: Stay ready and communicate. Handle or move the puck only when appropriate and permitted.
G.lose: Find the puck and adjust your position as the attacking threat develops.

gear: Protect your head and face. Ask an adult to check the helmet, face protection and straps.
Wear your mouthguard as your program requires; have an adult check its fit.
Neck protection belongs in your kit. Have an adult check the required type and fit.
These cover your shoulders and upper body.
These protect your elbows. Pack the pair.
These protect your hands while you hold your stick.
A properly fitted jock or jill is part of the kit.
Padded hockey pants cover the hips and upper legs.
Shin pads cover the knees and lower legs. Pack both.
Hockey socks go over your shin pads.
Ask an adult to check the fit and laces before you step on the ice.
Bring a stick that fits you. Your coach can help with the size.
Wear your jersey over your upper-body equipment.

signals.name: Holding
signals.cue: One hand grips the other wrist in front of the chest.
signals.meaning: A player restrains an opponent with a hand, arm or leg.

signals.name: Roughing
signals.cue: A closed fist extends away from the body, to the front or side.
signals.meaning: A player uses unnecessary rough physical contact against an opponent.

signals.name: Head contact
signals.cue: An open hand pats the side of the head.
signals.meaning: A player makes prohibited contact with an opponent’s head.

signals.name: Goal scored
signals.cue: One arm points toward the net where the puck went in.
signals.meaning: The official is indicating a goal.

signals.name: Interference
signals.cue: Both arms cross and stay still in front of the chest.
signals.meaning: A player illegally impedes an opponent who is not carrying the puck.

signals.name: Slashing
signals.cue: The edge of one hand chops across the opposite forearm.
signals.meaning: A player swings a stick at an opponent. Contact is not always needed.
